q: how does a nuclear fusion reactor work
how do fusion reactors produce energy
nuclear fusion power plant how it works
how does nuclear fusion generate electricity
how does a fusion reactor create energy
how does magnetic confinement fusion work
a: A nuclear fusion reactor aims to replicate the process that powers the Sun and stars: fusing light atomic nuclei together to release enormous amounts of energy. The most promising reaction for Earth-based fusion involves combining two isotopes of hydrogen — deuterium and tritium — to form helium-4 and a high-energy neutron. This reaction releases about 17.6 MeV of energy per fusion event, millions of times more energy per atom than chemical reactions like burning fossil fuels. The fundamental challenge is that atomic nuclei are positively charged and strongly repel each other via the Coulomb force. To overcome this repulsion and bring nuclei close enough for the strong nuclear force to take over, the fuel must be heated to extremely high temperatures — around 150 million degrees Celsius, about 10 times hotter than the core of the Sun. At these temperatures, matter exists as a plasma: a swirling, electrically charged gas of separated electrons and ions. No physical container can withstand such temperatures, so fusion reactors use magnetic confinement, with the tokamak design being the most advanced. A tokamak is a doughnut-shaped (toroidal) chamber surrounded by powerful superconducting magnets that create helical magnetic field lines. These fields confine and control the plasma, keeping it away from the walls and compressing it to sustain fusion conditions. Inside the reactor, the high-energy neutrons produced by fusion escape the magnetic confinement and are absorbed by the reactor wall (the blanket), where their kinetic energy is converted into heat. This heat is then transferred to a coolant (such as water or molten salt), which produces steam to drive turbines and generate electricity — similar to conventional power plants. The tritium fuel can be bred within the reactor by having the neutrons react with lithium in the blanket. The international ITER experiment in France is the largest tokamak ever built and aims to demonstrate net energy gain (Q > 10). Beyond tokamaks, alternative designs include stellarators, which use twisted magnetic fields for inherently stable plasma confinement, and inertial confinement fusion, which uses lasers to compress and heat tiny fuel pellets, as pursued at the National Ignition Facility. Despite enormous progress, practical commercial fusion power remains a significant engineering challenge, with issues including plasma stability, materials that can withstand neutron bombardment, and sustained tritium breeding still needing solutions.
